guideTitle: Best DIY Mini Split Air Conditioners (2026)
metaTitle: Best DIY Mini Split Air Conditioners (2026)
metaDescription: Six pre-charged DIY mini splits compared on quick-connect line sets, voltage, capacity and install effort, with honest notes on what you still must do.
expertTake: The Albott 12,000 BTU 115V DIY kit is the pick for most homeowners because it needs no new 230V circuit and keeps the refrigerant side sealed. The MRCOOL DIY Select 18,000 BTU is the value pick when a bigger room justifies the electrical work. If you are not comfortable cutting a wall hole and wiring a disconnect, skip the category and hire an installer.
introParagraphs: A DIY mini split ships with the refrigerant already sealed inside the outdoor unit and the line set, so you connect it with quick-connect fittings instead of a vacuum pump and gauges. That removes the hardest and most regulated step of a normal installation.

It does not remove everything. You still choose a wall location, drill the penetration, mount two units, drain the condensate and, on larger models, wire a dedicated circuit. Line set length and electrical supply are the details that make or break the project.

products.name: Albott 12,000 BTU 115V DIY Mini Split with Fast-Fit Set
products.description:
The Albott kit is built around a fast-fit line set and an indoor unit that arrives pre-wired, which cuts the on-site wiring to the power supply and the communication connection. As an inverter heat pump it modulates compressor speed, so you get both cooling and heating. Because it runs on 115V, you avoid the biggest hidden cost of a DIY installation, a new two-pole circuit.

The limit is capacity: 12,000 BTU covers a living room or a bedroom plus an open hall, but it will not carry a whole floor. Next to the MRCOOL DIY Select 18,000 BTU it gives up a third of the capacity in return for simpler electrical work, which for a typical home is the better trade.

In ownership, the quick-connect fittings are sealed once and should not be reopened, so plan the line set route carefully before you cut. The usual chores apply: a monthly filter rinse, a sloped drain, and keeping the outdoor coil clear. If you relocate the unit later, ask the maker whether the fittings can be reused. Before you order, decide where the outdoor unit will sit, since the line set length in the kit limits how far from the indoor head it can go. Many owners underestimate how much a clean, straight wall penetration matters for drain flow and for keeping the refrigerant lines free of kinks.
products.bestFor: A homeowner who wants a true DIY install on a standard 115V circuit.
pros: Pre-wired indoor unit reduces wiring steps
cons: Capacity tops out around a living room
Fittings are meant to be connected once
Line set length is fixed by the kit

products.name: Albott 12,000 BTU 220V DIY Mini Split, 18 SEER2
products.description:
This is the 220V version of the same Albott DIY platform, with the same fast-fit set and pre-wired indoor unit, and an 18 SEER2 efficiency rating. At 12,000 BTU it has the same capacity as the 115V Albott, so the only practical reason to choose it is that you already have a 220V circuit available, for example from a retired dryer or welder outlet.

Compared with the 115V model, the 220V draws about half the current for the same load, which allows a smaller breaker and thinner supply wire in some installs. That helps only when the run from the panel is long. If you have to pull a new two-pole circuit just for this unit, the 115V version is the cheaper project.

Ownership is the same as the 115V sibling. Keep the filters clean, the drain sloped and the outdoor coil clear, and mount the outdoor unit on a pad or a bracket that is level so the compressor oil returns properly.
products.bestFor: A homeowner who already has a spare 220V circuit near the install site.
pros: Same pre-wired fast-fit approach as the 115V Albott
Lower current draw for the same 12,000 BTU
Suits long runs from the panel
cons: A new 220V circuit adds cost if none exists
Same capacity as the cheaper 115V model
Needs level mounting for compressor oil return

products.name: ROVSUN 9,000 BTU 20 SEER2 115V Wi-Fi Mini Split
products.description:
The ROVSUN is the smallest and least expensive system here, a 9,000 BTU inverter heat pump with a 20 SEER2 rating and Wi-Fi control. The listing sells it on its quiet 28 dB mute mode and wide setpoint range, which suit a bedroom or a small office.

Be clear about what the listing does not promise. Unlike the Albott and MRCOOL kits, the data I have does not describe it as a pre-charged quick-connect system, so confirm the installation method before you count on a no-vacuum install. I include it for its value and because its line set options are common, but it is the one pick that may still need a technician.

At 9,000 BTU it is the right size for roughly 350 to 450 square feet. In a larger room it will run flat out and still miss the setpoint. Maintenance is the standard monthly filter rinse and a clear outdoor coil.
products.bestFor: A bedroom or small office where 9,000 BTU is enough and cost matters most.
pros: Lowest entry cost in this lineup
cons: Listing does not describe a no-vacuum install

products.name: MRCOOL DIY Select 18,000 BTU 230V Heat Pump
products.description:
MRCOOL's DIY Select line includes a pre-charged quick-connect line set, so the listing states you need no vacuum pump, gauges, brazing or refrigerant handling. The 18,000 BTU model is rated up to 800 square feet on 230V, with 17.3 SEER2 cooling efficiency and 8.5 HSPF2 heating efficiency.

The HSPF2 figure is useful, since it tells you how efficiently the unit heats over a season, and the 8.5 here is solid for a DIY-class system. Its cooling efficiency is lower than the 20 SEER2 ROVSUN, but that is the cost of a bigger compressor with a longer proven record. The 230V supply means a dedicated breaker, so you should include the electrical work in your budget.

In ownership terms, MRCOOL is a long-established DIY brand and parts and phone support are easier to reach than from the smallest sellers. The outdoor unit is heavier, so use a proper pad or heavy-duty bracket and keep the line set run within the length allowed for the factory charge. Because the wiring is on a larger circuit than the small units, hire a licensed electrician for the breaker and disconnect even if you handle every other step yourself, and keep the permit paperwork if your town requires it.
products.bestFor: An 800 square foot room or open area where a DIY install is wanted.
pros: Pre-charged line set means no vacuum pump
Rated for rooms up to 800 square feet
cons: Cooling efficiency trails the 20 SEER2 ROVSUN
Heavier outdoor unit needs a solid mount

products.name: MRCOOL DIY Select 24,000 BTU 230V Heat Pump
products.description:
The 24,000 BTU DIY Select steps up to a two-ton system rated for up to 1,050 square feet, with 16.5 SEER2 cooling efficiency and 8.3 HSPF2 heating efficiency. It keeps the pre-charged quick-connect line set that defines the DIY Select line, so the refrigerant side still needs no pump or gauges.

Efficiency slides as capacity rises, so this is less efficient than the 18,000 BTU sibling at 17.3 SEER2 and 8.5 HSPF2. You are paying for coverage, not for efficiency. One indoor head can only move so much air, so a single-wall unit serves an open floor well and closed bedrooms poorly.

The install demands heft: a bigger outdoor unit, thicker line set and a larger breaker. Plan the lift and the pad, and have a helper for mounting the outdoor unit. Maintenance mirrors the smaller units. Check the doorway and stair clearances before delivery, since the outdoor unit for a two-ton system is bulky enough that one person will struggle to carry it alone.
products.bestFor: An open floor plan, shop or garage up to about 1,000 square feet.
pros: Two-ton capacity for large open spaces
Rated for up to 1,050 square feet
cons: Lowest SEER2 in this lineup at 16.5
A single head cannot reach closed rooms

buyingCriteria.explanation: A DIY mini split must ship with refrigerant sealed in the outdoor unit and a pre-charged line set, which is what the MRCOOL DIY Select 18,000 BTU and 24,000 BTU listings state. Many cheap standard units look similar but require a vacuum pump, gauges and refrigerant handling that is regulated. Read the listing for the words pre-charged and quick connect before ordering.

The factory charge is sized for a specific line set length, and the MrCool Easy Pro lists 11.5 feet while the 36,000 BTU kit lists 25 feet. Exceeding the allowed length without adjusting the charge hurts efficiency and can damage the compressor. Measure the distance between your indoor and outdoor spots before choosing a kit.

The Albott 12,000 BTU 115V kit and ROVSUN 9,000 BTU run on a standard supply, while the MRCOOL 18,000 and 24,000 BTU units need 230V. A new two-pole circuit can cost as much as a small unit, and the work often must be done by a licensed electrician. Treat the electrical supply as part of the price.

About 20 BTU per square foot is the starting rule, so the 9,000 BTU ROVSUN fits around 400 square feet and the 12,000 BTU Albott roughly 600. The MRCOOL 18,000 BTU is rated to 800 square feet and the 24,000 BTU to 1,050. Oversizing causes short cycling and a clammy room.

If you will heat with the system, look at HSPF2 as well as SEER2. The MRCOOL 18,000 BTU shows 8.5 HSPF2 and the 24,000 BTU shows 8.3. A heat pump with a stated low-temperature limit and a good HSPF2 will cost less to run than electric baseboards over a winter.

buyingCriteria.criterion: What the kit does not include
buyingCriteria.explanation: A DIY kit still needs a wall bracket or pad, a disconnect box, wiring, a drain route and a mounting plate. Some listings include a condensate pump or a mounting kit and others do not. Add those parts and a day or two of labor to your plan. Make a written parts list from the manual before buying, because a missing disconnect or drain fitting stops the job for a day.

howWeEvaluated.title: DIY completeness
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked each listing for a pre-charged line set, quick-connect fittings and a pre-wired indoor unit. Kits that state a no-vacuum install scored highest, and the ROVSUN lost points because its listing does not state it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Electrical burden
howWeEvaluated.description: We scored the amount of electrical work each kit demands. The 115V Albott and ROVSUN need only a standard circuit, while the MRCOOL 18,000 and 24,000 BTU units require 230V. Less new wiring earned more points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the stated coverage with each unit's BTU rating. The MRCOOL 18,000 BTU covers 800 square feet while the 24,000 BTU covers 1,050. Honest coverage claims scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Efficiency figures
howWeEvaluated.description: We read SEER2 and HSPF2 together. The MRCOOL pair states 8.5 and 8.3 HSPF2 for heating, which makes them easier to judge as winter heat sources than units with no heating figure.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership support
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed brand history, warranty language and the availability of replacement parts based on owner feedback patterns. DIY systems have no installer to call, so manufacturer support matters more than usual.

cards.label: 115V
cards.text: The Albott 115V and ROVSUN plug into a dedicated standard circuit, which is the least expensive supply to provide. The price is a ceiling near 12,000 BTU.

cards.label: 220V to 230V
cards.text: The Albott 220V, MRCOOL 18,000 BTU and 24,000 BTU draw less current per BTU and allow bigger capacity. They require a two-pole breaker and heavier wire.

howToChoose.note: Choose 115V unless you need more than 12,000 BTU or already have a spare 220V circuit.

howToChoose.subheading: For a True No-Vacuum Install Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: The listing should say pre-charged, quick-connect and no vacuum pump. A pre-wired indoor unit is a further sign that the maker expects a homeowner install.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The MRCOOL DIY Select 18,000 and 24,000 BTU and the Albott 115V and 220V kits state this approach. The ROVSUN does not, so confirm before relying on it.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The space is large or you need real winter heat. The MRCOOL 18,000 BTU for an 800 square foot room or the 24,000 BTU for an open floor is worth the extra electrical work.

cards.text: The room is a bedroom or small office. The ROVSUN 9,000 BTU or the Albott 115V avoids a new circuit and still gives inverter efficiency.

maintenance.why: A clogged filter reduces airflow and can freeze the coil. Dry it fully before refitting.
A DIY drain route that sags will hold water and leak. Pour water into the pan to confirm it flows.
A slow leak shows as oily residue at the joint. Do not reopen sealed fittings without the maker's guidance.
Debris cuts airflow and raises pressure. Rinse gently from the inside out.
Vibration loosens bracket bolts over time. A loose outdoor unit rattles and stresses the line set.

faq.q: Is a DIY mini split really install-it-yourself?
faq.a: The refrigerant side is, because the line set is pre-charged and uses quick-connect fittings. You still mount two units, drill a wall hole, route a drain and wire power, which on 230V models is best done by a licensed electrician.

faq.q: Which DIY mini split is cheapest to install?
faq.a: A 115V kit like the Albott 12,000 BTU needs no new 230V circuit, so the installed cost stays lowest. Larger MRCOOL kits need a dedicated breaker and heavier wire. Also budget a few small parts such as a wall bracket, a weatherproof disconnect and a drain fitting, which are often sold separately.

faq.q: Does a longer line set hurt performance?
faq.a: Yes, if it exceeds the length the factory charge supports. Kits list set lengths such as 11.5 feet or 25 feet, and going beyond that without a charge adjustment lowers efficiency.

faq.q: Are DIY mini splits less efficient than professional ones?
faq.a: Not inherently. The MRCOOL 18,000 BTU lists 17.3 SEER2, which is competitive. DIY units do trade some efficiency for the convenience of quick-connect fittings and pre-charged sets.

faq.q: Will a DIY install void the warranty?
faq.a: Usually not for kits designed for DIY, but read the terms. Some warranties require a licensed electrician for the supply wiring or require proof of correct installation.

faq.q: Can I move a DIY mini split later?
faq.a: Quick-connect fittings are meant to be connected once. Ask the maker whether they can be reused, and expect that relocating may need a technician and new refrigerant.
